solution:
Take the rest mass of an electron as \(m_e = 9.10939 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg} = 9.10939 \times 10^{-28}\,\text{g}\).

(i) Number of electrons weighing 1 g

\(n = \dfrac{1\,\text{g}}{9.10939 \times 10^{-28}\,\text{g}} = 1.098 \times 10^{27}\) electrons

(ii) One mole contains \(N_A = 6.022 \times 10^{23}\) electrons.

Mass \(= (9.10939 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}) \times (6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 5.486 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{kg}\)

Charge \(= (1.602 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{C}) \times (6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 9.647 \times 10^{4}\,\text{C}\)

Answer: (i) \(1.098 \times 10^{27}\) electrons; (ii) mass \(= 5.486 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{kg}\) (\(0.5486\,\text{mg}\)), charge \(= 9.647 \times 10^{4}\,\text{C}\).

(i) One molecule of \(\text{CH}_4\) has \(6 + 4(1) = 10\) electrons, so one mole has

\(10 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 6.022 \times 10^{24}\) electrons.

(ii) \(^{14}\text{C}\) has molar mass \(14\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\) and \(14 - 6 = 8\) neutrons per atom.

Moles \(= \dfrac{7 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{g}}{14\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 5 \times 10^{-4}\,\text{mol}\); atoms \(= 3.011 \times 10^{20}\).

(a) Neutrons \(= 8 \times 3.011 \times 10^{20} = 2.409 \times 10^{21}\)

(b) Mass \(= (2.409 \times 10^{21})(1.675 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}) = 4.035 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{kg}\)

(iii) \(\text{NH}_3\) has molar mass \(17\,\text{g mol}^{-1}\) and \(7 + 3 = 10\) protons per molecule.

Moles \(= \dfrac{34 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{g}}{17\,\text{g mol}^{-1}} = 2 \times 10^{-3}\,\text{mol}\); molecules \(= 1.2044 \times 10^{21}\).

(a) Protons \(= 10 \times 1.2044 \times 10^{21} = 1.204 \times 10^{22}\)

(b) Mass \(= (1.204 \times 10^{22})(1.673 \times 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}) = 2.014 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{kg}\)

The answer does NOT change with temperature and pressure: the count of protons is fixed by the amount of substance taken (34 mg), and mass is independent of the state of the gas.

Answer: (i) \(6.022 \times 10^{24}\); (ii) \(2.409 \times 10^{21}\) neutrons, \(4.035 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{kg}\); (iii) \(1.204 \times 10^{22}\) protons, \(2.014 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{kg}\); no change with T and p.

The complete symbol is \(^{A}_{Z}\text{X}\), where the element is fixed by \(Z\).

(i) \(Z = 17\) is chlorine: \(^{35}_{17}\text{Cl}\)

(ii) \(Z = 92\) is uranium: \(^{233}_{92}\text{U}\)

(iii) \(Z = 4\) is beryllium: \(^{9}_{4}\text{Be}\)

The period \(T\) and frequency are reciprocals: \(\nu = 1/T\).

\(\nu = \dfrac{1}{2.0 \times 10^{-10}\,\text{s}} = 5.0 \times 10^{9}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{c}{\nu} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{5.0 \times 10^{9}\,\text{s}^{-1}} = 6.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\)

\(\bar{\nu} = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{6.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}} = 16.67\,\text{m}^{-1}\)

Answer: \(\lambda = 6.0 \times 10^{-2}\,\text{m}\) (6.0 cm), \(\nu = 5.0 \times 10^{9}\,\text{Hz}\), \(\bar{\nu} = 16.67\,\text{m}^{-1}\).

\(\lambda = 4000\,\text{pm} = 4000 \times 10^{-12}\,\text{m} = 4 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}\).

Energy of one photon

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1})}{4 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 4.97 \times 10^{-17}\,\text{J}\)

Number of photons giving 1 J

\(n = \dfrac{1\,\text{J}}{4.97 \times 10^{-17}\,\text{J}} = 2.01 \times 10^{16}\)

Answer: \(2.01 \times 10^{16}\) photons.

Einstein's photoelectric equation: \(h\nu = W_0 + \tfrac{1}{2}m_e v^2\).

(i) \(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{4 \times 10^{-7}} = 4.97 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

\(= \dfrac{4.97 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}}{1.6020 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J eV}^{-1}} = 3.10\,\text{eV}\)

(ii) Kinetic energy \(= 3.10 - 2.13 = 0.97\,\text{eV} = 1.56 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

(iii) \(v = \sqrt{\dfrac{2 \times 1.56 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}}{9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}}} = 5.85 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\)

Answer: (i) \(3.10\,\text{eV}\); (ii) \(0.97\,\text{eV}\) (\(1.56 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)); (iii) \(5.85 \times 10^{5}\,\text{m s}^{-1}\).

The ionisation energy per atom is the energy of one 242 nm photon.

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(3 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1})}{242 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}} = 8.21 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

Per mole

\(E = (8.21 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J})(6.022 \times 10^{23}\,\text{mol}^{-1}) = 4.95 \times 10^{5}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

Answer: \(494.7\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

\(\lambda = 0.57\,\mu\text{m} = 0.57 \times 10^{-6}\,\text{m}\).

Energy of one quantum

\(E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{0.57 \times 10^{-6}} = 3.487 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

The bulb supplies \(25\,\text{J s}^{-1}\), so the rate of emission of quanta is

\(\dfrac{25\,\text{J s}^{-1}}{3.487 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}} = 7.17 \times 10^{19}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

Answer: \(7.17 \times 10^{19}\) quanta per second.

Electrons leave with zero velocity, so the incident radiation is exactly at the threshold: \(\lambda_0 = 6800\,\text{Å} = 6.8 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\).

\(\nu_0 = \dfrac{c}{\lambda_0} = \dfrac{3.0 \times 10^{8}\,\text{m s}^{-1}}{6.8 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}} = 4.41 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}\)

\(W_0 = h\nu_0 = (6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s})(4.41 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}) = 2.92 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

\(= \dfrac{2.92 \times 10^{-19}}{1.602 \times 10^{-19}} = 1.82\,\text{eV}\)

Answer: \(\nu_0 = 4.41 \times 10^{14}\,\text{s}^{-1}\), \(W_0 = 2.92 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\) (\(1.82\,\text{eV}\)).

For hydrogen, \(\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}\left[\dfrac{1}{n_i^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_f^2}\right]\) with \(n_i = 4\), \(n_f = 2\).

\(\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\left[\dfrac{1}{16} - \dfrac{1}{4}\right] = -4.088 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

(negative, so energy is emitted). Taking the magnitude,

\(\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{|\Delta E|} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{4.088 \times 10^{-19}} = 4.86 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: \(\lambda = 486\,\text{nm}\) (visible, blue-green line of the Balmer series).

For hydrogen \(E_n = -\dfrac{2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{n^2}\,\text{J atom}^{-1}\). Ionisation means taking the electron to \(n = \infty\), where \(E = 0\), so the energy required is \(|E_n|\).

From \(n = 5\): \(E_5 = -\dfrac{2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{25} = -8.72 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J}\), so energy required \(= 8.72 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J atom}^{-1}\).

Per mole \(= (8.72 \times 10^{-20})(6.022 \times 10^{23}) = 52.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

From \(n = 1\) (the ionization enthalpy): \(2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J atom}^{-1} = 1312\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\).

Comparison: the ratio is \(\dfrac{2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{8.72 \times 10^{-20}} = 25\), i.e. \(n^2\).

Answer: \(8.72 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J atom}^{-1}\) (\(52.5\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)) — only \(1/25\) of the ionization enthalpy of the H atom, because the \(n = 5\) electron is far less tightly bound.

An electron in level \(n\) can reach the ground state by any downward route, so the number of distinct spectral lines is the number of pairs of levels from \(n\) down to 1:

\(\text{lines} = \dfrac{n(n-1)}{2}\)

For \(n = 6\): \(\dfrac{6 \times 5}{2} = 15\).

Answer: 15 emission lines.

[Textbook answer-key error of sign, and THE QUESTION'S OWN STEM REFUTES IT. The key prints the fifth-orbit energy as a POSITIVE quantity — but the stem itself supplies the first-orbit energy as \(-2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J atom}^{-1}\), negative, and \(E_n = E_1/n^2\) divides that by \(25\), an operation that cannot change its sign. So the key contradicts the datum printed in the question it answers. The physics agrees: an electron bound in an atom has negative total energy by construction, the zero of the scale being the free electron at rest, which is exactly why ionisation requires energy to be supplied. Only the sign is at issue; the magnitude the key prints, \(8.72 \times 10^{-20}\), is correct.] For hydrogen \(E_n = \dfrac{E_1}{n^2}\) and \(r_n = (0.0529\,\text{nm})n^2\).

(i) \(E_5 = \dfrac{-2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}}{5^2} = -8.72 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J atom}^{-1}\)

(ii) \(r_5 = (0.0529\,\text{nm})(25) = 1.3225\,\text{nm} = 1.3225 \times 10^{-9}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: (i) \(-8.72 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J atom}^{-1}\); (ii) \(1.3225\,\text{nm}\) (\(132.25\,\text{pm}\)).

The Balmer series ends at \(n = 2\). The LONGEST wavelength corresponds to the SMALLEST energy gap, i.e. the transition from the nearest level, \(n = 3 \rightarrow n = 2\).

Rydberg equation: \(\bar{\nu} = R_H\left[\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right]\), \(R_H = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\,\text{m}^{-1}\)

\(\bar{\nu} = 1.097 \times 10^{7}\left[\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{9}\right] = 1.097 \times 10^{7} \times 0.1389 = 1.523 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m}^{-1}\)

Answer: \(\bar{\nu} = 1.523 \times 10^{6}\,\text{m}^{-1}\) (\(1.523 \times 10^{4}\,\text{cm}^{-1}\); \(\lambda \approx 656\,\text{nm}\)).

[Textbook answer-key error, self-refuting against the key's own second figure. The key prints the energy required as \(2.08 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{ergs}\); the question's own datum gives \(2.18 \times 10^{-11} \times (1 - 1/25) = 2.0928 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{ergs}\), which neither rounds nor truncates to 2.08. The key refutes itself in the same entry: it goes on to print a wavelength of \(950\,\text{Å}\), and \(2.0928 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{ergs}\) corresponds to \(949.8\,\text{Å}\) while its own \(2.08 \times 10^{-11}\) would give \(956\,\text{Å}\). So the wavelength it prints is the one our energy produces, not the one its own energy produces.] \(E_1 = -2.18 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{erg} = -2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}\) (since \(1\,\text{erg} = 10^{-7}\,\text{J}\)).

\(E_5 = \dfrac{E_1}{25} = -8.72 \times 10^{-20}\,\text{J}\)

Energy required for \(n = 1 \rightarrow n = 5\):

\(\Delta E = E_5 - E_1 = -8.72 \times 10^{-20} + 2.18 \times 10^{-18} = 2.093 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}\)

On returning to the ground state the same energy is emitted as one photon:

\(\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{2.093 \times 10^{-18}} = 9.50 \times 10^{-8}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: \(\Delta E = 2.093 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}\); \(\lambda = 95.0\,\text{nm}\) (\(950\,\text{Å}\), ultraviolet — the Lyman series).

\(E_2 = \dfrac{-2.18 \times 10^{-18}}{2^2} = -5.45 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

Complete removal means going to \(n = \infty\) where \(E = 0\), so

\(\Delta E = 0 - (-5.45 \times 10^{-19}) = 5.45 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\)

The LONGEST wavelength that can still cause this transition is the one whose photon energy is exactly \(\Delta E\):

\(\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{\Delta E} = \dfrac{(6.626 \times 10^{-34})(3 \times 10^{8})}{5.45 \times 10^{-19}} = 3.647 \times 10^{-7}\,\text{m}\)

\(= 3.647 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{cm}\)

Answer: energy \(= 5.45 \times 10^{-19}\,\text{J}\); \(\lambda = 3.647 \times 10^{-5}\,\text{cm}\).

de Broglie relation \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m v}\), with \(m_e = 9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg}\).

\(\lambda = \dfrac{6.626 \times 10^{-34}\,\text{J s}}{(9.11 \times 10^{-31}\,\text{kg})(2.05 \times 10^{7}\,\text{m s}^{-1})} = 3.55 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\)

Answer: \(\lambda = 3.55 \times 10^{-11}\,\text{m}\) (\(35.5\,\text{pm}\)).

[Textbook answer-key error, self-refuting on the chapter's own rule. The key prints the two isoelectronic sets as \(\text{Na}^{+}, \text{Mg}^{2+}, \text{Ca}^{2+}\) and \(\text{Ar}, \text{S}^{2-}, \text{K}^{+}\), placing \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) with the ten-electron species. Counting by the chapter's own rule (electrons \(= Z -\) charge), calcium has \(Z = 20\) so \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) has \(20 - 2 = 18\) electrons and belongs with \(\text{Ar}\) (18), \(\text{S}^{2-}\) (16 + 2 = 18) and \(\text{K}^{+}\) (19 - 1 = 18), while only \(\text{Na}^{+}\) (10) and \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) (10) form the ten-electron set. The answer below gives the corrected grouping with the electron count shown for every species so the reader can check it directly.] Count the electrons in each species (electrons \(= Z -\) charge).

| Species | \(Z\) | Electrons |
|---|---|---|
| \(\text{Na}^{+}\) | 11 | 10 |
| \(\text{K}^{+}\) | 19 | 18 |
| \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) | 12 | 10 |
| \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\) | 20 | 18 |
| \(\text{S}^{2-}\) | 16 | 18 |
| \(\text{Ar}\) | 18 | 18 |

Answer: two isoelectronic sets — \(\text{Na}^{+}\) and \(\text{Mg}^{2+}\) (10 electrons each), and \(\text{K}^{+}\), \(\text{Ca}^{2+}\), \(\text{S}^{2-}\) and \(\text{Ar}\) (18 electrons each).

(i) Add or remove electrons from the neutral atom and fill in order of increasing energy.

\(\text{H}^{-}\) (2 e): \(1s^2\)

\(\text{Na}^{+}\) (10 e): \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\)

\(\text{O}^{2-}\) (10 e): \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\)

\(\text{F}^{-}\) (10 e): \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\)

(ii) Complete the configuration up to the stated outermost electrons and count.

(a) \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^1\) gives \(Z = 11\) (Na)

(b) \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^3\) gives \(Z = 7\) (N)

(c) \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^5\) gives \(Z = 17\) (Cl)

(iii) Expand the core and count the electrons.

(a) \([\text{He}]\,2s^1\) is 3 electrons — lithium (Li)

(b) \([\text{Ne}]\,3s^2\,3p^3\) is 15 electrons — phosphorus (P)

(c) \([\text{Ar}]\,4s^2\,3d^1\) is 21 electrons — scandium (Sc)

A \(g\) subshell has azimuthal quantum number \(l = 4\) (\(s, p, d, f, g\) correspond to \(l = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4\)).

For a given \(n\), \(l\) can take values \(0\) to \(n - 1\), so \(l = 4\) requires \(n - 1 \geq 4\), i.e. \(n \geq 5\).

Answer: \(n = 5\).

"\(3d\)" fixes the principal and azimuthal quantum numbers: the digit 3 gives \(n = 3\) and the letter \(d\) gives \(l = 2\).

For a given \(l\), \(m_l\) runs from \(-l\) to \(+l\).

Answer: \(n = 3\), \(l = 2\), and \(m_l = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2\) (five possible values, one per \(3d\) orbital).

The species is an ATOM, so it is electrically neutral and the number of protons equals the number of electrons.

(i) Protons \(= 29\), so \(Z = 29\) — the element is copper. (The 35 neutrons give \(A = 29 + 35 = 64\), i.e. \(^{64}_{29}\text{Cu}\).)

(ii) Filling by the Aufbau order gives \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,4s^2\,3d^9\), but copper is one of the two exceptions in the first transition series: a completely filled \(3d\) subshell is more stable than a filled \(4s\) with \(3d^9\), so one \(4s\) electron shifts to \(3d\).

Answer: (i) 29 protons; (ii) \(1s^2\,2s^2\,2p^6\,3s^2\,3p^6\,3d^{10}\,4s^1\), i.e. \([\text{Ar}]\,3d^{10}\,4s^1\).

Add the electrons of the constituent atoms and adjust for the charge.

\(\text{H}_2^{+}\): \(2 \times 1 - 1 = 1\) electron

\(\text{H}_2\): \(2 \times 1 = 2\) electrons

\(\text{O}_2^{+}\): \(2 \times 8 - 1 = 15\) electrons

Answer: 1, 2 and 15 electrons respectively.

The rules are \(l = 0\) to \(n - 1\), and \(m_l = -l\) to \(+l\).

(i) For \(n = 3\): \(l = 0, 1, 2\).

\(l = 0\): \(m_l = 0\)

\(l = 1\): \(m_l = -1, 0, +1\)

\(l = 2\): \(m_l = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2\)

(nine \(m_l\) values in all, i.e. \(n^2 = 9\) orbitals)

(ii) For a \(3d\) orbital: \(l = 2\) and \(m_l = -2, -1, 0, +1, +2\).

(iii) An orbital is possible only if \(l \leq n - 1\).

\(1p\): \(n = 1\) allows only \(l = 0\), so NOT possible.

\(2s\): \(n = 2\), \(l = 0\) — possible.

\(2p\): \(n = 2\), \(l = 1\) — possible.

\(3f\): \(f\) needs \(l = 3\), but \(n = 3\) allows only up to \(l = 2\), so NOT possible.

Answer: (iii) only \(2s\) and \(2p\) are possible.

The value of \(l\) fixes the letter: \(l = 0 \rightarrow s\), \(l = 1 \rightarrow p\), \(l = 2 \rightarrow d\), \(l = 3 \rightarrow f\); the value of \(n\) is written in front.

(a) \(n = 1\), \(l = 0\) — \(1s\)

(b) \(n = 3\), \(l = 1\) — \(3p\)

(c) \(n = 4\), \(l = 2\) — \(4d\)

(d) \(n = 4\), \(l = 3\) — \(4f\)
_note: The stem says 'Using s, p, d notations', but part (d) has l = 3 and can only be named with the f notation. Answered with 4f.

solution:
The constraints are \(n \geq 1\) (an integer), \(l = 0\) to \(n - 1\), \(m_l = -l\) to \(+l\), and \(m_s = \pm\tfrac{1}{2}\).

(a) NOT possible — \(n\) cannot be 0; the principal quantum number starts at 1.

(b) Possible — \(n = 1\) allows \(l = 0\), which allows only \(m_l = 0\).

(c) NOT possible — with \(n = 1\) the only permitted value is \(l = 0\), so \(l = 1\) is disallowed.

(d) Possible — \(n = 2\) allows \(l = 1\), and \(m_l = 0\) lies in \(-1\) to \(+1\).

(e) NOT possible — with \(n = 3\), \(l\) can be at most 2, so \(l = 3\) is disallowed.

(f) Possible — \(n = 3\) allows \(l = 1\), and \(m_l = 0\) lies in \(-1\) to \(+1\).

Answer: (a), (c) and (e) are not possible; (b), (d) and (f) are.

(a) A shell with principal quantum number \(n\) holds \(2n^2\) electrons. For \(n = 4\) that is \(2(4)^2 = 32\) electrons. By the Pauli principle each orbital holds one electron with \(m_s = +\tfrac{1}{2}\) and one with \(m_s = -\tfrac{1}{2}\), so exactly half carry \(m_s = -\tfrac{1}{2}\).

\(\dfrac{32}{2} = 16\) electrons

(b) \(n = 3\), \(l = 0\) is the \(3s\) subshell. A subshell with azimuthal quantum number \(l\) has \(2l + 1 = 1\) orbital, which holds 2 electrons.

Answer: (a) 16 electrons; (b) 2 electrons.

Bohr's quantisation condition states that the angular momentum of the electron in an allowed orbit is an integral multiple of \(h/2\pi\):

\(m v r = \dfrac{n h}{2\pi}\), \(n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots\)

Rearrange to isolate the circumference \(2\pi r\):

\(2\pi r = \dfrac{n h}{m v}\)

By the de Broglie relation the wavelength of the revolving electron is \(\lambda = \dfrac{h}{m v}\). Substituting,

\(2\pi r = n \lambda\)

Hence the circumference of the Bohr orbit is an integral multiple of the de Broglie wavelength — the electron wave closes on itself after \(n\) whole wavelengths, which is the standing-wave condition that makes the orbit stable.

For a hydrogen-like species of nuclear charge \(Z\),

\(\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,Z^2\left[\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2}\right]\,\text{J}\)

For \(\text{He}^{+}\) (\(Z = 2\)), the \(n = 4 \rightarrow n = 2\) transition gives

\(\Delta E = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times 4 \left[\dfrac{1}{4} - \dfrac{1}{16}\right] = 2.18 \times 10^{-18} \times 4 \times 0.1875 = 1.635 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}\)

The same wavelength means the same \(\Delta E\). For hydrogen (\(Z = 1\)) we need

\(\dfrac{1}{n_1^2} - \dfrac{1}{n_2^2} = \dfrac{1.635 \times 10^{-18}}{2.18 \times 10^{-18}} = 0.75\)

This is satisfied by \(n_1 = 1\), \(n_2 = 2\), since \(1 - \tfrac{1}{4} = 0.75\).

Answer: the \(n = 2 \rightarrow n = 1\) transition in hydrogen (the first line of the Lyman series).

\(\text{He}^{+}\) is a one-electron (hydrogen-like) species with \(Z = 2\), so

\(E_n = -\dfrac{(2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J})Z^2}{n^2}\)

The process removes the last electron from the ground state (\(n = 1\)) to \(n = \infty\), so the energy required is \(|E_1|\):

\(E = (2.18 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J}) \times \dfrac{2^2}{1^2} = 8.72 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J atom}^{-1}\)

Per mole

\(E = (8.72 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J})(6.022 \times 10^{23}\,\text{mol}^{-1}) = 5.25 \times 10^{6}\,\text{J mol}^{-1}\)

Answer: \(8.72 \times 10^{-18}\,\text{J atom}^{-1}\), i.e. \(5.25 \times 10^{3}\,\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\) — four times the value for hydrogen, because the energy scales as \(Z^2\).
